newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba denounces U.S., says Clinton sells EU short.
newsitem.headline: Cuba denounces U.S., says Clinton sells EU short.

text.p: Cuba mounted a new diplomatic offensive on Friday against U.S. moves to toughen restrictions on business with the communist-ruled island.

Parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon denounced attempts in the U.S. Congress to harden up the Helms-Burton law against Cuba, saying the Clinton administration was not fulfilling an agreement with the European Union to ease part of the law. He told a news conference Havana would raise the matter at the United Nations.
Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina addressed the foreign diplomatic corps on the issue on Thursday afternoon and was holding separate meetings with each EU ambassador on Friday.

By mounting an energetic diplomatic offensive, President Fidel Castro's government clearly sought to draw the EU's attention to what it sees as a lack of commitment by President Bill Clinton to fulfilling his April understanding with the EU on seeking to ease parts of Helms-Burton.

"What we are now considering are new steps in Washington that are specially directed against other countries and against the alleged understanding between the United States and the European Union," Alarcon said, adding that the congressional moves had so far been kept secret.

Cuba's indignation was based on a series of Cuba-related amendments to a wider bill on foreign relations approved on May 6 by the House of Representatives International Relations Committee. The amendments seek to add to the Helms-Burton law or to modify earlier legislation concerning Cuba.
Cuba also objects to two draft bills prepared by the House panel that seek to strengthen Helms-Burton in other ways.

Alarcon said the Clinton administration was doing nothing to stop the passage of amendments that contradicted the spirit of the agreement with the EU. He added he had the impression that to date the administration "has done absolutely nothing (to fulfil the understanding)."

Under the April understanding Europe agreed to suspend a World Trade Organisation (WTO) challenge to Helms-Burton. In return Washington agreed to seek to change a key Helms-Burton provision barring from the United States executives of foreign companies deemed to be doing business on property expropriated from U.S. citizens or firms after Castro's 1959 revolution.

The moves in Congress include a proposal to tie full funding of aid to Russia to assurances it has ended aid to nuclear projects in Cuba. Another requires the State Department to file quarterly reports to Congress on implementation of Helms-Burton sanctions.

The agreement between the EU and Washington helped resolve trans-Atlantic tensions over Helms-Burton, which was rapidly approved by Clinton in March 1996 following the downing by Cuba of two small private U.S. planes off the island.
The law, adding to a 35-year U.S. embargo on Havana, drew international criticism over its provisions affecting third country firms doing business in Cuba.

Alarcon noted that even if the understanding with the EU were to be fulfilled, Cuba would still oppose Helms-Burton, which, apart from its provisions on foreign firms, seeks a radical political overhaul in Cuba. He cited "its illegal character and its deep anti-Cuban sense."
